title: Dipoles, verticals and wire antennas
blurb: Size a dipole or monopole from frequency, and explain how pattern and feed impedance change with height, feed position and radials.

G9B01.why: With no feed line to contain RF, **station equipment may carry significant RF current**.
G9B01.trap: A random wire has no required length, polarization or band preference.

G9B02.why: **Sloping the radials downward** raises the low feed impedance of a flat ground plane toward 50 Ω.
G9B02.trap: Sloping them up or coiling them doesn't help.

G9B03.why: A quarter-wave vertical radiates equally in every compass direction: **omnidirectional in azimuth**.
G9B03.trap: Not isotropic: it still favors the horizon over straight up.

G9B04.why: In the plane of the wire a dipole is a **figure-eight at right angles to the wire**. Nulls are off the ends.
G9B04.trap: The lobes are broadside, not off the ends.

G9B05.why: Under **½ λ** high, much of the energy goes steeply up, where the figure-eight fills in: the azimuth pattern is **almost omnidirectional**.

G9B06.why: Radials go **on the ground or buried a few inches**, where they collect the return currents.
G9B06.trap: Raised, vertical or centered radials are the wrong place for a ground-mounted vertical.

G9B07.why: Nearing ground, the reflection partly cancels the antenna: feed impedance **steadily decreases**.

G9B08.why: Current falls and voltage rises toward the ends, so impedance **steadily increases** as the feed point moves out.

G9B09.why: A horizontal antenna doesn't push return currents through lossy soil, so it has **lower ground losses**.

G9B12.why: A quarter-wave monopole is 234 ÷ 28.5 = 8.2, about **8 ft**.
